marks: Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir settled in this valley, united the scattered Yazidi tribes and returned to them their ancient temple; his tomb is the holiest Yazidi site.
An Ottoman army under Melek Ahmed Pasha stormed the mountain in 1640; Evliya Çelebi reports that 3,060 Yazidis were killed.
Yazidi captives taken to Rawanduz in 1832, among them the Mîr Ali Beg, were executed here when they refused to convert to Islam.
700 Yazidi cavalry fought with the Armenian force that stopped the Ottoman advance in May 1918.
The Islamic State captured Sinjar in August 2014 and began the genocide of the Yazidis: over 5,000 were killed and thousands of women and girls enslaved.
The largest Yazidi temple in the world, Quba Mere Diwane, opened here in 2019.
notes: Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir settles at Lalish, unites the scattered Yazidi tribes and reforms their religion; after his death (1162) his nephew leads the community.
Sheikh Hasan brings the Sheikhan principality to its height and founds a Council of Holy Men; the ruler of Mosul has him killed (1246).
Yazidism is the religion of many Kurdish tribes and emirates, from Antioch to Sulaymaniyah; its lands form seven centres, each with its sacred sinjaq.
Sunni Kurdish tribes ransack Lalish (1414); many Yazidi chiefs are forcibly converted, and Yazidi power declines.
Under Ottoman rule Hussein Beg briefly governs Erbil (1534); fatwas of the Sheikh al-Islam legitimise the killing and enslavement of Yazidis (1566).
Ottoman expeditions strike the Yazidis of Shingal: in 1613 the Yazidis defeat them, but in 1640 an army storms Mount Sinjar and kills 3,060.
Ottoman campaigns against Sinjar and Sheikhan follow one another, some fifteen in the 18th century alone.
Muhammad Pasha of Rawanduz massacres the Yazidis of Sheikhan (1832); Yazidis flee to the Russian Empire, and in 1892 Lalish is turned into a madrasa.
Yazidis are killed in the Armenian genocide and flee to Transcaucasia; in the later 20th century many emigrate from Turkey to Germany.
The Islamic State captures Sinjar (2014): over 5,000 Yazidis are killed, thousands of women and girls enslaved and more than 500,000 flee.
src: John S. Guest, Survival Among the Kurds: A History of the Yezidis (1993)
